notes.AL: You demonstrate a solid understanding of the AI as a summarization and translation tool. You instruct it to format information specifically for your own external workflow, requesting it to "Explain these in short, simple language, for my notes copy pasting".
notes.PR: Your prompts are clear in their constraints ("without losing any information", "without missing any kind of detail, since exams questions might come from any part"). However, your problem decomposition is less structured than in Chat 2, as you rely heavily on repetitive, generic instructions like "now this, similarly, as above" and "Now explain this, as done above" as you feed it new images.
notes.AUI: You exhibit a strong instinct for cognitive augmentation by testing your own mental models against the AI's understanding. You attempt to build intuition around a Naive Bayes feature vector by summarizing it yourself and asking the AI to validate it: "ok, summarise, so, for example, in this image, this 1 tells. that this word was present in the mail... and 0 means... is this true ?".
notes.EC: While you proactively verify your own logic with the AI ("is this true ?"), there is less evidence of you actively challenging the AI's mathematical reasoning on complex topics like Kernel methods and SVMs. However, you do engage actively with its conceptual analogies, playfully acknowledging its explanation of SVM slack variables with "okay, i allow some mistakes".
notes.CS: You successfully merge multiple dense textbook excerpts covering diverse machine learning topics (Naive Bayes event models, Laplace smoothing, Least Mean Squares, Support Vector Machines) while maintaining a consistent instructional format tailored for your revision notes.
notes.CD: Your interaction pattern in this session is highly convergent and repetitive. You are methodically working through textbook pages using the exact same prompt structure ("explain tthis", "now this") to extract standardized explanations, showing little to no non-obvious thinking or exploration.
notes.ES: Ethical concerns regarding bias or societal consequences do not apply to your study of mathematical classification algorithms like SVM and Naive Bayes.
notes.CA: You maintain strong cognitive ownership over the session's direction. You drive the ingestion of the textbook pages and dictate exactly how the AI should present the information to serve your "notes copy pasting" workflow.
